properties.name: Colombia's Congress: the parapolitics convictions
properties.group: Convicted, or found by a court
properties.what the record says: Since the scandal broke in 2006, more than 60 congressmen and seven governors have been convicted for using paramilitary intimidation to get elected; some 140 more former congressmen were under investigation (Colombia Reports). Human Rights Watch counted more than 55 current and former members of Congress convicted by its 2014 report. Paramilitaries had signed pacts with politicians to 'refound the motherland'. Demobilised paramilitaries named close to a thousand politicians as accomplices (InSight Crime). In 2024 León Valencia, whose research helped open the cases, counted 86 members of Congress convicted and 50 more investigated: 136, which he describes as half of Congress (Publimetro).
properties.source: Compiled for this map on 28 September 2026 from the sources listed

properties.name: Colombia's Congress after parapolitics: candidates with ties to illegal groups elected
properties.group: Documented ties, funding, or laws written for them
properties.what the record says: Of 131 candidates questioned for criminal ties by the Peace and Reconciliation Foundation, 69 won seats (33 Senate, 36 Chamber): investigated for direct ties with criminal groups, or connected to politicians accused or convicted of parapolitics.

properties.name: Japan's ruling party and the Unification Church
properties.group: Documented ties, funding, or laws written for them

properties.what the record says: The Liberal Democratic Party's own survey (September 2022): 179 of its 379 national lawmakers had ties with the church and related groups, from attending events to receiving election help; 17 received election help. The party named 121 with substantial ties. The survey did not cover local assembly members.

properties.name: Qatargate: Antonio Panzeri and Francesco Giorgi (European Parliament)
properties.group: Admitted by the person, or by the side that paid or ran them

properties.name: Canada's Parliament: members said to assist foreign states (NSICOP report)
properties.group: Found by an official inquiry
properties.working for or tied to: China and India, among others (unnamed parliamentarians)
properties.what the record says: The National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians (June 2024) wrote that some elected officials 'began wittingly assisting foreign state actors soon after their election'. It named no one publicly. The public inquiry that followed (Justice Hogue) found the situation 'not as clear cut, nor as extreme' as the report's wording suggested.

properties.name: United States: state laws copied from bills written by industry and advocacy groups
properties.group: Documented ties, funding, or laws written for them
properties.working for or tied to: Industry groups, ALEC and other model-bill writers
properties.what the record says: USA Today, the Arizona Republic and the Center for Public Integrity compared nearly a million bills: at least 10,000 bills introduced over eight years were copied almost entirely from model legislation, and more than 2,100 became law. By author: 4,301 industry, 4,012 conservative groups, 1,602 liberal groups, 248 others. Placed at the middle of the country: it covers all 50 state legislatures.

properties.name: West Germany: the Stasi's agents and wiretaps
properties.group: Named in opened secret-police or spy-service files
properties.what the record says: The Stasi's foreign intelligence service recruited 20,000 to 30,000 agents in West Germany during the Cold War, and listened to the phone calls of the West German president, the heads of its security services, senior officials in Bonn and all members of the Bundestag (CIA review of the Stasi archive's own study). In 2010 the Stasi archive was asked to check about 2,000 people who sat in the Bundestag between 1949 and 1989.

He ruled Panama 1983–1989.

properties.name: The kids-for-cash judges: Mark Ciavarella and Michael Conahan (Luzerne County, Pennsylvania)
properties.group: Convicted, or found by a court
properties.working for or tied to: The builder and co-owner of two for-profit youth detention centres
properties.what the record says: The judges shut the county's own juvenile detention centre and took $2.8 million in illegal payments from the builder and co-owner of two private lockups, then filled them with children. Ciavarella was convicted of racketeering (28 years); Conahan pleaded guilty. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court threw out about 4,000 of Ciavarella's juvenile rulings (2003–2008).
properties.source: Compiled for this map on 28 September 2026 from the sources listed

properties.name: Odebrecht's bribes to officials in Angola
properties.group: Admitted by the person, or by the side that paid or ran them
properties.what the record says: In its December 2016 guilty plea in the United States, Odebrecht admitted paying about $788 million in bribes to officials and political parties, through a division that worked as a bribery department, for more than 100 projects in twelve countries (Angola, Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Guatemala, Mexico, Mozambique, Panama, Peru, Venezuela), from 2001 to 2016, gaining about $3.336 billion. This point marks the officials of Angola; the plea does not name them.
